title: Subsequent Events
description: Determine whether events after year-end require adjustment, disclosure, or no action.
html:
Subsequent Events

Subsequent events are events or transactions that occur after the balance sheet date but before the financial statements are issued or available to be issued.

CPA Focus:

The key question is whether the event provides additional evidence about conditions that already existed at the balance sheet date, or whether it relates to conditions that arose after year-end.

1. Recognized Subsequent Events

A recognized subsequent event provides additional evidence about a condition that existed at the balance sheet date.

The financial statements are adjusted to reflect the effect of the event.

Condition Existed at Year-End Adjust Financial Statements
Example — Customer Bankruptcy

A major customer declares bankruptcy shortly after year-end.

Evidence shows the customer was already experiencing serious financial difficulty before December 31.

The bankruptcy provides additional evidence about the collectibility of the receivable that existed at year-end.

Existing Year-End Condition → Recognized Subsequent Event → Adjust Financial Statements

2. Nonrecognized Subsequent Events

A nonrecognized subsequent event relates to a condition that arose after the balance sheet date.

The financial statements are generally not adjusted for the event.

However, material events may require disclosure so that the financial statements are not misleading.

Condition Arose After Year-End Generally No Adjustment
Example — Fire After Year-End

A company's manufacturing facility is destroyed by a fire on January 20.

There was no condition related to the fire at December 31.

The fire is therefore generally a nonrecognized subsequent event.

If the event is material, appropriate disclosure may still be necessary.

3. Recognized vs. Nonrecognized

Evidence About Existing Condition Recognize / Adjust
New Condition After Year-End Do Not Adjust

4. Lawsuit Example

Assume a lawsuit existed before year-end. Shortly after year-end, the company reaches a settlement that confirms the amount of the obligation at the balance sheet date.

The settlement may provide additional evidence about the year-end liability and therefore may require adjustment.

5. New Borrowing After Year-End

Assume a company enters into a major new borrowing agreement after the balance sheet date.

If the borrowing relates to a new condition arising after year-end, it generally does not change the liabilities reported at the earlier balance sheet date.

Material information may still require disclosure.

6. Major Business Combination

A major acquisition completed after year-end is generally a nonrecognized subsequent event if the underlying transaction arose after the balance sheet date.

Because such a transaction could significantly influence users' decisions, disclosure may be required when material.

7. Subsequent Event Evaluation Period

Management evaluates subsequent events through the applicable date the financial statements are issued or available to be issued.

The applicable evaluation date depends on the entity's reporting circumstances. Some entities evaluate subsequent events through the date the financial statements are issued, while others evaluate them through the date the financial statements are available to be issued.

CPA Exam Decision Rule

Did the condition exist at the balance sheet date? YES ↓ Recognized Subsequent Event ↓ Adjust NO ↓ Nonrecognized Subsequent Event ↓ No Adjustment + Disclose if Material

Key Takeaways

  • Subsequent events occur after the balance sheet date but before the financial statements are issued or available to be issued.
  • Events providing additional evidence about existing year-end conditions generally require adjustment.
  • Events caused by conditions arising after year-end generally do not require adjustment.
  • Material nonrecognized subsequent events may require disclosure.
  • Customer bankruptcy may be recognized when it confirms financial difficulty that already existed at year-end.
  • A major fire occurring entirely after year-end is generally nonrecognized.

quiz.prompt: A customer owing a company $90,000 declares bankruptcy shortly after year-end. Evidence indicates the customer was already experiencing severe financial difficulty at the balance sheet date. How should the company generally treat this subsequent event?

choices.text: Ignore the event because bankruptcy occurred after year-end
Recognize the effect by adjusting the year-end financial statements
Record the loss only in the following year
Report the $90,000 as other comprehensive income

quiz.explanation: The bankruptcy provides additional evidence about a condition that already existed at the balance sheet date. Therefore, the year-end financial statements should generally be adjusted.
